rows.en: But the investigator would waste his time in vain⚠1 if he sought a particular order and system for each of these two Houses, for these men were simple in their ways; they knew no systematic structures of learning, but went along in innocence in their exposition. Yet this cannot be denied: from the sum of their disputes it emerges for us that each of these two Houses had a particular leaning in its learning. In various matters that we have from the House of Hillel the characteristic is recorded and explicit: in clarifying their opinion they would often add a reason for their words, and sometimes they would also give a reason for the words of their opponents, so that it was said of them (Eruvin 13b) that for this reason the House of Hillel merited that the halakhah be according to them against the House of Shammai, their colleagues.{v1_10_05:1} The House of Hillel very greatly wished not to make the Torah a burden on those who keep it; rather they strove to lighten the load of the commandments for the sake of the good order of the world.{v1_10_05:2} Their footsteps were known in the ways of Hillel's traits, which are the traits of kindness and of setting people's minds at ease, and these traits also shine through their teachings. In many of their halakhot we have seen that they decided the law only according to the measure of kindness and of doing good to people.{v1_10_05:3} Above all, their eye was always on the moral law and the spiritual thought in the statutes of the Torah. This is revealed and seen from their opinion concerning the bond of marriage. They held that this bond is tied only with cords of love and by free will. According to the law of the Torah the father had the right to give his minor or adolescent daughter in betrothal (Kiddushin 2:1); such betrothals were binding, and she had no power to refuse them: against her will she was betrothed and against her will she must keep them, for so they understood the plain sense of Scripture. But for a minor girl who has no father, the sages gave her mother or her brothers the right to marry her off with her consent, or even without her consent (Yevamot 107b); this was a settled halakhah in the days of the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel. This custom was established for her benefit. For in their time and in their land they were accustomed to marry off their daughters while they were minors, and therefore, for the advantage of the minor who has no father, they gave the right to her mother and her brothers. But if she refuses the husband whom her mother and brothers designated for her, she has the right to annul the betrothal. Now the halakhah of refusal (mi'un) was fixed with regard to a betrothed girl, but they were in doubt what her law is with regard to a married girl. Likewise the halakhah was not fixed for the case where the husband died and she had not refused, and she fell before the levir: whether she has the right to refuse the levir. Nor was the halakhah fixed whether this refusal must be in the presence of the husband and in a court, or also not in his presence and not in a court. On all these matters the House of Hillel made their opinion known in a way from which it appears that they strove to remove, as far as possible, compulsion and constraint from matters of marriage. Therefore they made it a law that even if she had been married off in a full marriage and her soul does not desire her husband, she may refuse and annul the marriage; and not only with a husband but also with a levir she may refuse. And lest her heart be faint and she be ashamed to refuse him in his presence, or be ashamed to go to a court, and so unwillingly load upon herself the yoke of compulsion and not refuse, while her heart will not be with her husband all the days of her life, they made it a law that she may refuse even not in his presence and not in a court (Yevamot 13:1). This spirit also governs the law of divorce in the system of the House of Hillel. The House of Shammai did not permit the husband to divorce his wife unless he found in her some unseemly matter [Deuteronomy 24:1], and in no other way does he have the right to divorce her, even if the husband sees, after he has brought her into his home, that she has qualities of soul or body that are not fit to win his love, and he knows in himself that he will never find contentment and domestic peace in her company. Even so he has no right to send her away from his house, but against his will he must say of the joining, "It is good" [Isaiah 41:7], while in his heart "it is bad, it is bad," he will say of it [Proverbs 20:14]. Without doubt they decided thus because they believed in a divine decree spread over every individual person and over each individual one of his deeds; for from of old the saying was held among the people that forty days before the forming of the child it is decreed in heaven who will be his or her mate (Sanhedrin 22a). Therefore the bond of marriage was in their eyes a bond tied in heaven, and it is not fitting that man should untie it unless religion and the Torah require its untying. But this view was not fit to establish the happiness of man in general and the peace of the home in particular, and if it were put into practice it would easily become a cause of the corruption of morals. The House of Hillel did not think so, for they said: the Torah wishes by its statutes to found morality and purity of life, and it would not give a law through which danger and harm to morality could come; the law of divorce would be harmful to morality if it were limited as the House of Shammai limit it, but it would be of great benefit to morality, to man's happiness and to the peace of the home if it gave the husband the right to divorce his wife for anything he found in her that is not according to his soul and his will, and that would become a cause of hatred instead of his loving her. The trait of kindness they kept even where the law compelled them to decide a judgment to punish a person, and in every possible way they lessened the measure of his punishment.{v1_10_06:1} Now, since these foundations were their foundations, it is self-evident that they did not readily agree to decree decrees, and if they found even a small reason to refrain from decreeing a decree, they refrained and had no misgivings;{v1_10_06:2} and they went one step further, in that at times they permitted evading a prohibition by means of a stratagem (Pesaḥim 36a, and the Tosafot there). In all these characteristics the way of the House of Hillel was marked, and the House of Shammai the reverse.

rows.en: In a great number of their disputes on matters of halakhah they made it their aim to clarify old halakhot: either to explain their meaning and reason,{v1_10_06:3} or to define their conditions,{v1_10_06:4} or to extend them;{v1_10_06:5} and if we consider their sayings we will find that most of their disputes on halakhah fall into these kinds. Their way of clarifying and explaining the old halakhot was the same as the way that each side chose for itself in clarifying Scripture. The House of Shammai did not depart from the meaning of the words as written in interpreting the Torah, while the House of Hillel went deep into the intent of the verse and decided by weighing with their judgment and by reasoning.{v1_10_06:6} Their interpretations in understanding the halakhot received from their predecessors are also marked by this characteristic. The House of Shammai held every received halakhah to be like planted nails [Ecclesiastes 12:11], from which one may in no way move even when reasoning requires a deviation; and therefore it is self-evident that this way caused the House of Shammai not to cease giving precept upon precept [Isaiah 28:10] and decreeing decree upon decree, and therefore the House of Shammai were always among the stringent. But the House of Hillel refrained⚠1 wherever possible, on the basis of reasoning and weighing of judgment, so as to distinguish between cases, and for this reason they could for the most part lean to the side of leniency.

1.note: Print reads נמנעו ('refrained'); the sense fits poorly; perhaps a misprint for a verb like 'strove'.

rows.en: The length of time that the two Houses continued we cannot define precisely, for we do not know when Shammai's house of study was founded, or when he became head of the court (av beit din). But this is clear: the division of the Houses did not continue beyond the time of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai. And if after the destruction we still find some traces of the existence of sages of the House of Shammai, this is no sign that the Houses continued in force one against the other; for even if the association was dissolved, it does not follow that in one moment all its parts would dissolve and change their opinion. It is true that individual men lived even after the destruction who did not depart from their former opinion, but on that account we cannot call them by the name of a House. Therefore the later sages called the House of Shammai by the title "the first generations," as against R. Dosa ben Harkinas, whom they called by the title "the last generations" (Gittin 81a), although this R. Dosa lived in the time of the Temple and after it (Yevamot 16a). It is true that there are a very few of the disputes between the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel that appear from their content to be children of the time after the destruction; but from this there is no proof that the Houses existed after the destruction. For if we look at the foundations of those halakhot, we will find that nothing compels us to attach the dispute only to the time when the Temple was gone; rather one can find a place for those disputes also while the Temple stood, and the later sages after the destruction attached the disputes to examples fitting their own time. Of this kind we find two disputes. The first: one who had produce in this time, and the time of removal arrived: the House of Shammai say he must redeem it for money, and the House of Hillel say, it is all one whether it is money or produce (Ma'aser Sheni 5:7). The core of this dispute is from the time of the Temple. For at various times they could not bring up the second tithe to Jerusalem because of the disorder of the roads and the wars, and the sages of the Houses disagreed whether this falls under "the place is too far" [Deuteronomy 14:24] (see *Tosafot Yom Tov*); and the later sages who received this halakhah phrased it as fitted their own time.{v1_10_07:1} So we find in several of their disputes that the later sages reported things from them in a way that seems to us as though the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel said so; but it is not so: rather the formulations were formulated by the later sages, who put them thus in the mouth of the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel.{v1_10_07:2} The second dispute: the House of Shammai say: one who says, "I take upon myself a marḥeshet" — it shall be left until Elijah comes; and the House of Hillel say: there was a vessel in the Temple and its name was marḥeshet (Menaḥot 63a). From the outer form of this dispute one may judge, and it has already been judged (*Darkhei ha-Mishnah* p. 54), that it is from the time after the destruction of the Temple. But this dispute too, by its content, is possible in the time of the Temple. Someone vowed while the Temple stood, in the words "I take upon myself a marḥeshet," and asks how he is to fulfil this vow: surely one who is in doubt about the meaning of the word marḥeshet, and does not know whether marḥeshet is named after its making, so that the vessel is called marḥeshet because a meal-offering called marḥeshet is baked in it, or whether marḥeshet is the name of the vessel itself, cannot give his questioner a clear answer, but must leave the matter in doubt. The House of Shammai, who were in doubt, were therefore forced to say: it shall be left until Elijah comes; but the House of Hillel, for whom it was clear that marḥeshet is the name of the vessel, therefore oblige the one who vowed to bring such a vessel to the Temple. Now, what is it that compels us to say that this dispute is from the time after the destruction? Nothing but the outer form of the saying of the House of Hillel, who said: "there was a vessel in the Temple." But who will tell us that this is not just a formulation that was formulated at a late time? Surely it is so, for anyone versed in the language of the early Tannaim will understand that the formulation of this dispute, as it was formulated in our Babylonian Talmud, is not original, and bears on its forehead a stamp that was stamped in the late period. The truth is that these disputes were transmitted by one of the disciples of the House of Shammai who still lived after the destruction, or that the sayings here called in the name of the House of Shammai were said by one of his disciples after the destruction, and they called them by the name of the House of Shammai. Therefore in no case can one bring a proof from this for the existence of the Houses; and in particular it is hard to picture the matter of the two Houses from the death of Shammai and Hillel onward. The House of Hillel remained in existence, for from the seed of Hillel came the Patriarchs and the heads of the Sanhedrin and of learning. But what became of the House of Shammai after the death of its head? Had there been a separate house of study, someone must have stood at its head, and how is it that it is not mentioned who the head was? This compels us to think that they had no separate house of study; rather, after the death of Shammai a great number of his disciples remained alive for a long time, and they are called by the name House of Shammai. In some halakhot we can recognize from their content which of them are from the time of Shammai and Hillel. Every dispute in which, as we know, the opinion of Shammai himself leans to the opinion of the House of Hillel, or is neither like these nor like those, but he had a separate opinion — such a dispute is from a late time. For example, in their dispute about impure leaven that leavened the dough, what its measure is (Orlah 2:4), where one of Shammai's disciples testified that he heard from his master the measure of the House of Hillel (ibid. 2:5): this dispute is from a late time. And perhaps also in other places (Eduyot 1:7, 8, 10, 11) where the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel disagree and Shammai had another opinion, the House of Shammai departed from the opinion of their master without knowing it, and only one of the disciples knew it and made it known to his colleagues. And we find a dispute between the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel in which Hillel spoke neither like these nor like those, but it is said: "Hillel for his part used to say such and such," that is, he remained alone in his opinion (Ma'aserot 4:2 and Tosefta ch. 3). In this it is explicitly hinted that it was so in his time, and that his colleagues and disciples did not agree with him. In their dispute whether one lays hands on a voluntary burnt-offering on a festival (Beitzah 2:4 and parallels), it is clear that they disagreed so in the days of Hillel (Yerushalmi Ḥagigah ch. 2 and Tosefta ch. 2). In one dispute in which the House of Hillel retracted to rule like the House of Shammai, it appears that this was in the time of Shammai and Hillel. It is this (Yevamot 115b): the House of Shammai say she may remarry on her own testimony and collect her ketubbah; and the House of Hillel say she may remarry but may not collect her ketubbah. Why did they say she may not collect her ketubbah? Because they did not expound the wording of the ketubbah, in which it is written, "When you are married to another, you will take what is written for you." And why did they not expound it? Because Hillel their master too did not expound it. But Hillel changed his mind and expounded it. Therefore it appears that as long as Hillel did not expound it, his disciples too did not expound it, and there was a dispute between the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel; and when Hillel changed his mind and expounded it, his disciples too expounded the wording of the ketubbah and retracted to rule like the words of the House of Shammai (see Yerushalmi Ketubbot ch. 4 and Tosefta ch. 4, and Yevamot (116a)⚠1 with the Tosafot). Likewise their dispute whether one may vow an oath to murderers, to confiscators and to tax-collectors, where the House of Shammai say one may not swear and the House of Hillel say one may swear (Nedarim ch. 3), was also in the time of Shammai and Hillel, because of an event that happened: Herod, seeing that the heart of the people was not faithful to him, issued a decree that every single man must enter into a sworn oath to be loyal to their king, and those who refused to swear he punished with a fine of money or in their bodies. Shammai and Hillel and the sect of the Essenes he did not make swear, for he trusted in the character of their spirit, that they were lovers of peace (*Antiquities* 15, ch. 10). About six thousand refused to swear, and he punished them with money (17, ch. 2). Without doubt, because of this event they were roused to this question and disagreed in their opinions. Those who refused to swear were of the House of Shammai, and they said that one may not swear. Where the elders of the House of Shammai and the elders of the House of Hillel are mentioned, this does not refer to Shammai and Hillel themselves; rather the distinguished men of the Houses were called elders (Sukkah 2:6⚠2; Tosefta Rosh ha-Shanah ch. 2; Menaḥot 41a; *Darkhei ha-Mishnah* p. 55). Among the multitude of their disputes we find no more than eight in civil law and no more than four in the laws of sacrifices.{v1_10_08:1} The reason is that the performance of the sacrifices was entrusted to the priests, and they knew the details of the procedure, it being a thing practised every day; and the disputes on the laws of sacrifices among the later sages came about because after the destruction the sacrificial service ceased and the laws were forgotten. Civil law was entrusted to the courts, and the sages of exposition left it to the judges who were appointed to establish justice. For this reason we do not find that they disagreed on the laws of the Sanhedrin, nor on punishments for transgressions. In particular it appears that most of their disputes are on matters that concern the individual Jew and on laws that are in the hands of every person. Nor is there any dispute between them on the laws of the Megillah and its reading, nor on the laws of fasts, of the sotah and of skin-afflictions (*Darkhei ha-Mishnah* p. 55).

Ohalot 2:3, two halakhot; 5:1, 2, 3, and the House of Hillel retracted, see Eduyot 1:14; and 7:2, two halakhot, see Tosefta ch. 8; 11:1, see Tosefta ch. 12; 11:3, among the leniencies of the House of Shammai; 11:4, among the leniencies of the House of Shammai; 11:5, 6, and all of them are among the leniencies of the House of Shammai, and in Eduyot they were counted only as one, since they have one reason; 11:8; 13:1, 4; 15:8; Tosefta ch. 15, see in the Mishnah 15:9; ch. 16, see in the Mishnah 16:4. Parah 12:10, see Tosefta ch. 11. Tohorot 9:5, 7; 10:4. Mikva'ot 1:5; 4:5, see R. Samson, from whom it appears that the House of Hillel disagree; 5:6, and it is among the leniencies of the House of Shammai according to R. Judah, Eduyot 5:2 and Tosefta ch. 4. Makhshirin 1:2, 3, 4; 5:4; 5:5, two halakhot (in 5:9 it is not found that the House of Hillel disagreed). Zavim 1:1, 2; Tosefta ch. 1, five halakhot. Tevul Yom 1:1; Tosefta ch. 2, three halakhot according to R. Judah and R. Yoḥanan ben Beroka⚠1. Uktzin 3:6, two halakhot, the aforementioned I have already counted, and one is among the leniencies of the House of Shammai; 3:8; 3:11.

1.note: Abbreviations; ר"י may be R. Judah or R. Yose, and ריב"ב R. Yoḥanan ben Beroka or R. Judah ben Betera.

footnotes.en: Niddah 2:4, 6; 6:4; Gemara (71a); 6:6, 7, 8, two halakhot. Kelim 9:8, and the House of Hillel retracted, see Eduyot ch. 1; 11:3; Tosefta ch. 2. Ohalot 18:1, 4, 8. Parah, Tosefta ch. 4, see Mishnah 5:1. Tohorot, Tosefta ch. 8. Mikva'ot 4:1; 10:6.

The remaining disputes in which the House of Hillel are stringent: see Eduyot 1:14, and they retracted; three in 5:1 according to R. Judah; one in mishnah 4 according to R. Ishmael; one in mishnah 8 according to R. Eliezer; one in mishnah 2 according to R. Yose; and all of them are in halakhah and in midrash. In Eduyot twenty-four are counted among the leniencies of the House of Shammai, and the Talmud and its commentators noticed that the number is not exact; see Yoma (80a), Yerushalmi Pe'ah 6:2, and the Tosafot on Ketubbot (78a) and Kiddushin (2a). Sometimes the author of the Gemara reverses the reading, see Bekhorot (30b); and in the Tosefta Demai ch. 2 the reading follows the correction of the Bavli; and in the Tosefta Terumot ch. 2 the House of Shammai are also lenient, and in the Yerushalmi 3:4 it reverses the reading; and see Yevamot (28a), Ḥullin (105a), and see Kilayim 6:1, *Tosafot Yom Tov*, and Ma'aser Sheni 4:8. But all the answers do not help to deny the fact that matters are found in which the House of Shammai are lenient that were not counted in the Mishnah.

Rashi there brought a proof from Berakhot 1:3. And in Shevi'it 1:1 the House of Hillel explain the measure of the House of Shammai. The clarification of the House of Hillel explains the unstated view of the House of Shammai, for example: a person who is placed under the crack — the House of Shammai say he does not bring the impurity; and from what the House of Hillel said, "a person is hollow," it is made explicit that the reason of the House of Shammai is that there is no hollow of a handbreadth in him.

Ḥagigah (7b–8a): that the House of Hillel permitted the festival-offering of the first festival day of Passover from the tithe. And in Gittin (55a) and the Tosefta Bava Kamma ch. 10 they made an enactment for the benefit of penitents. One may feed the poor with demai and guests with demai (Shabbat 127b), to make the commandment of charity easier and to make it easier for hosts (Maimonides on Demai 3:1).

So it emerges from their dispute in Ketubbot (59b) about a woman who vowed not to nurse her son. Also out of the trait of kindness they enacted that a large amount is not required for betrothal money, but a perutah suffices, to make it easier for the poor man (Kiddushin 1:1); and they permitted altering the truth to set people's minds at ease (Ketubbot 17a).

Their dispute about one who misappropriates a deposit, where the House of Hillel say: [he pays] as at the time of taking it out (Bava Metzia 3:12); and about one who intends to misappropriate it (ibid.).

Demai 1:6: the House of Hillel held that one may sell his olives for tithe, and we do not fear that they will exude liquid,⚠1 for wherever we can attribute, we attribute. See Shevi'it 5:8 concerning the sale of a cow, and in the Tosefta ch. 4 concerning the sale of fields and ch. 6 concerning the sale of Sabbatical-year produce; and in Shabbat (18b) concerning selling his article to a gentile; and see further there 1:7 and 8, and in Avodah Zarah (15b).

1.note: Compressed phrase; rendered as 'we do not fear that they will exude liquid [and become susceptible], since we attribute'; שתולין is unclear.

footnotes.en: Berakhot 8:1: the old halakhah was to bless over the day and over the wine, and they disagreed which comes first. In Shabbat 3:1 the old halakhah: "a stove that was heated ... one may not put [food on it] until he sweeps it out," and they disagreed what one may put. See further Berakhot 8:2, 3, 4; Beitzah 2:1; Pesaḥim 1:1; Kilayim 4:1; 10:1⚠1; Yevamot (80a): the halakhah that a eunuch and an aylonit have no ḥalitzah and no levirate marriage, and they disagreed about its meaning.

1.note: Kilayim has only nine chapters; reference kept as printed.

footnotes.en: Shevi'it 1:1: the old halakhah: one ploughs in a grain-field on the eve of the Sabbatical year, and they disagreed about its limits. Terumot 1:4: one does not separate terumah from olives for oil, and they disagreed about its limits. See further Ma'aser Sheni 4:8; 5:6; Yevamot 3:1; Yerushalmi Shabbat 1:3, on sending a letter, and the Bavli (19a); in the Yerushalmi 1:8, on setting sail in a ship; and in the Mishnah 3:1 they disagreed whether one may take and put back. And see Ḥullin 1:2: the old halakhah is that one does not slaughter with a harvesting sickle, and they disagreed about its limits.
Shevi'it 8:3: one does not sell Sabbatical-year produce by measure, and they disagreed about bundles. Ma'aser Sheni 2:3 and 4; 5:7. Orlah 2:4.

Berakhot 1:3. Pe'ah ch. 6: the House of Shammai say three [sheaves] belong to the poor, and the House of Hillel say two; the reason of the House of Shammai is that it is written, "for the stranger, for the orphan and for the widow" [Deuteronomy 24:19], which makes three; and the House of Hillel judged by reasoning that the Torah was concerned for the stranger and the poor, as with gleanings and pe'ah, and Scripture speaks of the usual case; and see there in the Yerushalmi. 7:6: the House of Shammai say that a vineyard in its fourth year has no fifth, because it is not written explicitly, and this is "the words as they are written." Ma'aser Sheni 5:3 and Tosefta Terumot ch. 3. Shabbat 1:5: the House of Shammai say, "Six days shall you labour etc." [Exodus 20:9], that all your work be finished on the eve of the Sabbath — the words as they are written; and the House of Hillel say, "six days shall work be done" [Exodus 35:2], that work may be done all six days — so it is in the Tosefta ch. 1, and in the Yerushalmi there is another reading. Ibid. (135a): the House of Shammai say that one born circumcised must have the blood of the covenant drawn, for they expounded "the flesh of his foreskin" [Genesis 17:14] as actual flesh, even when there is no foreskin — the words as they are written; and the House of Hillel say that the Torah was concerned only with the cutting of the foreskin, and if there is no foreskin there is no circumcision. See Tosefta ch. 16, Yerushalmi Yevamot 8:1 and Sifra Tazri'a ch. 1. And in Yoma (61a) the House of Shammai hold, concerning a hairless nazirite, that we require the verse as it is written. See further Gittin 9:10; Bava Metzia (44a), on misappropriating a deposit; Ḥullin (88b), on covering blood with ashes; Bekhorot (32b, 33b), on a blemished firstling for outsiders and for menstruants; and so it is in most of the midrashim on which they disagreed.

See in the Tosefta Ma'aser Sheni ch. 3 the parallel of the halakhah in the Mishnah; and in the Yerushalmi at the end of ch. 1 of Ma'aser Sheni the reading follows the words of the House of Shammai, and this is correct.

See Tosefta Zavim ch. 1: "When R. Akiva was arranging halakhot for his disciples etc. R. Simeon said: Thus did the House of Hillel say to the House of Shammai"; there it is proven that these are not the words of the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel themselves, but R. Simeon put them thus in their mouths. I do not need many proofs, for one versed in the baraitot and the Talmuds will find it so in many places.
